ask.changes_what: Heavy pack-year history should raise COPD/ILD on the dyspnea differential and prompt spirometry once stable; it does not discriminate the acute cause.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use pack-years to attribute acute dyspnea to COPD when PE, ACS, pneumothorax, or heart failure are plausible.
ask.escalation_warning: Heavy smokers with acute chest pain or dyspnea need ACS and PE considered independently of COPD history.

evidence.citation: Straus SE, McAlister FA, Sackett DL, Deeks JJ. The accuracy of patient history, wheezing, and laryngeal measurements in diagnosing obstructive airway disease. CARE-COAD1 Group. JAMA. 2000;283(14):1853-1857.
evidence.population: 309 consecutive adults at 25 primary care and referral sites in 14 countries; 25% known OAD, 37% suspected, 39% neither
evidence.quote: smoking for more than 40 pack-years (LR, 8.3), self-reported history of chronic OAD (LR, 7.3)
evidence.reference_standard: Spirometry: FEV1 and FEV1/FVC ratio < 5th percentile adjusted for height, age, sex
evidence.target_condition: Obstructive airway disease (FEV1 and FEV1/FVC below 5th percentile) - finding: smoking >40 pack-years

ask.how: Ask packs per day and years smoked; pack-years = packs/day x years (20 cigarettes = 1 pack). Record current vs former status and quit date. Thresholds studied: >40 pack-years (CARE-COAD1) and >=70 pack-years (Badgett).
ask.negative_finding: Absence of heavy smoking does not exclude airflow limitation; the LR for absence was not reported in the abstract.
ask.pitfalls: Pack-year recall is imprecise; the finding predicts chronic OAD, not whether today's dyspnea is a COPD exacerbation versus pneumonia, ACS, or PE. Heavy smoking also raises probability of ACS, lung cancer and ILD.
ask.positive_finding: >40 pack-years strongly favours obstructive airway disease (LR 8.3) in patients with known, suspected, or no OAD; with prior COPD diagnosis, >=70 pack-years plus prior diagnosis had specificity 100%.
ask.prerequisites: Reliable history from patient or informant.
ask.title: Smoking history: >40 (or >=70) pack-years, current smoker

ask.changes_what: New orthopnoea raises probability of decompensated HF and supports BNP/echo and decongestion; absence should not be used to exclude HF.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not rely on the absence of orthopnoea to exclude heart failure, and do not attribute orthopnoea to heart failure without examining for tamponade, effusion or neuromuscular weakness when the picture does not fit.
ask.escalation_warning: Orthopnoea with hypotension, pulsus paradoxus or a raised JVP suggests tamponade or acute pump failure; obtain immediate echo.

evidence.citation: Fonseca C, Morais H, Mota T, et al. The diagnosis of heart failure in primary care: value of symptoms and signs. Eur J Heart Fail. 2004;6(6):795-800.
evidence.population: Portuguese primary care attendees screened by Boston questionnaire and referred for echocardiography (n=1058 assessed); orthopnoea sensitivity reported only as <36%
evidence.quote: a history of paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea (LR 35.5), orthopnea (LR 39.1) and breathlessness when walking on the flat (LR 25.8)
evidence.target_condition: Heart failure (cardiac dysfunction at rest on echocardiography)

evidence.citation: Ekundayo OJ, Howard VJ, Safford MM, et al. Value of orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and medications in prospective population studies of incident heart failure. Am J Cardiol. 2009;104(2):259-264.
evidence.population: 5,771 community-dwelling adults >=65 years in the Cardiovascular Health Study; 272 with adjudicated definite HF
evidence.quote: for either orthopnea or PND were 52% (95% confidence interval [CI] 46% to 58%), 83% (95% CI 82% to 84%)
evidence.reference_standard: Centrally adjudicated definite heart failure (CHS criteria)
evidence.target_condition: Prevalent definite heart failure (composite symptom: orthopnoea OR paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea)

ask.how: Ask whether breathing worsens within minutes of lying flat and eases on sitting up, how many pillows (or what head-of-bed angle) are needed to sleep, and whether this is new or increased compared with baseline. Distinguish from positional dyspnoea due to abdominal distension, obesity, or nasal obstruction, and from cough-related waking.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of orthopnoea only modestly lowers the probability of heart failure; many heart failure patients, particularly with chronic disease, sleep flat.
ask.pitfalls: Orthopnoea also occurs with COPD, massive ascites, obesity, and bilateral diaphragm paralysis; pillow count is confounded by habit, reflux and sinus disease. In chronic HF orthopnoea correlates poorly with measured wedge pressure.
ask.positive_finding: New or worsening need to sleep propped up, with dyspnoea on lying flat that resolves on sitting, points to raised left-sided filling pressure (heart failure) or, less often, tamponade, large effusion or bilateral diaphragm weakness.
ask.prerequisites: Patient (or collateral historian) able to describe sleep position and recent change.
ask.title: Orthopnea: dyspnea lying flat relieved by sitting up / number of pillows

ask.changes_what: Positive: de-emphasize ACS and work up PE/pneumonia/pneumothorax/pericarditis (exam, CXR, PE risk score). Negative: does not remove PE from the differential.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use pleuritic quality to discharge a patient with possible ACS without an ECG and troponin.
ask.escalation_warning: Pleuritic pain with hypoxemia, tachycardia, unilateral leg swelling or hemoptysis warrants immediate PE work-up; with sudden dyspnea consider pneumothorax.

evidence.citation: Panju AA, Hemmelgarn BR, Guyatt GH, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient having a myocardial infarction? JAMA. 1998;280(14):1256-1263.
evidence.population: Adults with acute chest pain in studies pooled by the RCE review
evidence.reference_standard: Confirmed MI by study criteria (enzymes/ECG) in included studies

evidence.citation: Courtney DM, Kline JA, Kabrhel C, et al. Clinical features from the history and physical examination that predict the presence or absence of pulmonary embolism in symptomatic emergency department patients: results of a prospective, multicenter study. Ann Emerg Med. 2010;55(4):307-315.
evidence.population: 7,940 symptomatic US ED patients tested for PE (12 centers); mean age 49, 67% female
evidence.quote: those with an adjusted odds ratio (OR) greater than 1.5 included non-cancer-related thrombophilia (OR 1.99), pleuritic chest pain (OR 1.53)
evidence.reference_standard: Imaging-confirmed PE or DVT within 45 days
evidence.target_condition: Venous thromboembolism (PE or DVT) in ED patients evaluated for PE

ask.how: Ask whether the pain is sharp and clearly worse with a deep breath, cough or sneeze (not with exertion or palpation), and whether there has been any hemoptysis. Ask separately about onset, exertional relation and positional relief so the pleuritic quality is not conflated with other descriptors.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of pleuritic quality does not exclude PE, pericarditis or pneumonia; PE frequently presents with isolated dyspnea or collapse without pleuritic pain.
ask.pitfalls: Pleuritic pain lowers but does not exclude ACS; no history element alone permits discharge without testing. Patients may label any sharp pain as breath-related unless asked specifically about inspiration.
ask.positive_finding: Pleuritic pain lowers the probability of myocardial infarction (LR about 0.2) and shifts the differential toward pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, pneumothorax, pericarditis and pleural disease. In ED patients evaluated for PE it modestly raises VTE probability (adjusted OR 1.5).
ask.prerequisites: Patient able to give a history; ask before analgesia if feasible.
ask.title: Pleuritic chest pain (sharp, worse with inspiration/cough), +/- hemoptysis

ask.changes_what: PND raises probability of decompensated HF (pooled LR+ ~2.6 in ED) and supports BNP/echo; absence changes little.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use absence of PND to exclude heart failure; do not label nocturnal wheeze as asthma in an older patient with risk factors for heart failure without checking for congestion.
ask.escalation_warning: PND with chest pain, new oedema or hypoxaemia at rest indicates decompensation that needs same-day assessment rather than outpatient follow-up.

evidence.citation: Wang CS, FitzGerald JM, Schulzer M, Mak E, Ayas NT. Does this dyspneic patient in the emergency department have congestive heart failure? JAMA. 2005;294(15):1944-1956.
evidence.population: Adults presenting to the emergency department with dyspnoea (22 studies pooled)
evidence.quote: the symptom of paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (positive LR = 2.6; 95% CI, 1.5-4.5)
evidence.reference_standard: Clinical diagnosis of heart failure adjudicated in the primary studies (varied criteria)
evidence.target_condition: Heart failure as cause of acute dyspnoea

evidence.citation: Fonseca C, Morais H, Mota T, et al. The diagnosis of heart failure in primary care: value of symptoms and signs. Eur J Heart Fail. 2004;6(6):795-800.
evidence.population: Portuguese primary care attendees screened by Boston questionnaire and referred for echocardiography (n=1058 assessed); PND sensitivity reported only as <36%
evidence.quote: a history of paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea (LR 35.5), orthopnea (LR 39.1) and breathlessness when walking on the flat (LR 25.8)
evidence.target_condition: Heart failure (cardiac dysfunction at rest on echocardiography)

evidence.citation: Ekundayo OJ, Howard VJ, Safford MM, et al. Value of orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and medications in prospective population studies of incident heart failure. Am J Cardiol. 2009;104(2):259-264.
evidence.population: 5,771 community-dwelling adults >=65 years in the Cardiovascular Health Study; 272 with adjudicated definite HF
evidence.quote: for either orthopnea or PND were 52% (95% confidence interval [CI] 46% to 58%), 83% (95% CI 82% to 84%)
evidence.reference_standard: Centrally adjudicated definite heart failure (CHS criteria)
evidence.target_condition: Prevalent definite heart failure (composite symptom: orthopnoea OR paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea)

ask.how: Ask whether the patient wakes from sleep, typically 1-3 hours after lying down, gasping or short of breath and has to sit up, stand or go to a window for relief that takes 10-30 minutes. Ask about wheeze or cough with the episodes and about daytime exertional dyspnoea, orthopnoea and oedema to separate cardiac from asthmatic nocturnal symptoms.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of PND is common in heart failure and provides little reassurance; it should not lower the probability enough to stop the work-up.
ask.pitfalls: Nocturnal asthma, COPD with secretions, sleep apnoea, reflux/aspiration and nocturnal angina produce similar waking; 'cardiac asthma' with wheeze is easily mislabelled as asthma. Recall is unreliable and prevalence is low so specificity drives its value.
ask.positive_finding: Episodes of waking from sleep with dyspnoea that resolve slowly on sitting or standing indicate redistribution of fluid into the lungs from raised left-sided filling pressure, i.e. decompensated heart failure.
ask.prerequisites: Patient or bed partner able to describe nocturnal episodes.
ask.title: Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea: waking 1-3 h after sleep with dyspnea relieved by sitting/standing

examine.changes_what: Diffuse wheeze: treat airflow limitation and confirm with spirometry/peak flow; new wheeze with edema/JVP elevation should prompt evaluation for heart failure rather than bronchodilators alone.
examine.contraindications: None, but avoid repeated forced expirations in a patient near exhaustion.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use absence of wheeze to exclude severe asthma or COPD exacerbation, or to exclude heart failure or pulmonary embolism as the cause of dyspnea.
examine.escalation_warning: Silent chest, inability to speak, drowsiness or stridor with wheeze (possible anaphylaxis or upper-airway obstruction) requires immediate airway and resuscitation measures.

evidence.citation: Straus SE, McAlister FA, Sackett DL, Deeks JJ; CARE-COAD1 Group. The accuracy of patient history, wheezing, and laryngeal measurements in diagnosing obstructive airway disease. JAMA. 2000;283(14):1853-1857.
evidence.population: 309 consecutive patients at 25 primary care and referral sites in 14 countries (25% known, 37% suspected OAD); 52% had OAD
evidence.quote: The LR for wheezing was 2.7 (95% confidence interval [CI], 1.7-4.2)
evidence.reference_standard: Spirometry: FEV1 and FEV1/FVC below 5th percentile adjusted for height, age and sex

evidence.citation: Arts L, Lim EHT, van de Ven PM, Heunks L, Tuinman PR. The diagnostic accuracy of lung auscultation in adult patients with acute pulmonary pathologies: a meta-analysis. Sci Rep. 2020;10:7347.
evidence.population: Adults with known or suspected COPD/asthma, 10 studies

evidence.citation: Arts L, Lim EHT, van de Ven PM, Heunks L, Tuinman PR. The diagnostic accuracy of lung auscultation in adult patients with acute pulmonary pathologies: a meta-analysis. Sci Rep. 2020;10:7347.
evidence.reference_standard: Doppler echocardiography, Framingham criteria or expert panel
evidence.target_condition: Congestive heart failure (cardiogenic pulmonary edema) - wheezes

examine.how: Auscultate all lung fields during tidal breathing and then during a forced expiration, noting whether wheeze is diffuse and polyphonic (airflow limitation) or focal and monophonic (localized obstruction). Listen over the neck to separate inspiratory stridor from expiratory wheeze.
examine.negative_finding: No wheeze does not exclude airflow limitation (sensitivity roughly 0.25-0.3); a 'silent chest' in a distressed asthmatic indicates critically low airflow, not improvement.
examine.pitfalls: Wheeze occurs in heart failure ('cardiac asthma') and pneumonia and does not discriminate them; its intensity does not track severity. Sensitivity is low and pooled specificity for obstructive disease around 0.9.
examine.positive_finding: Diffuse polyphonic expiratory wheeze supports airflow limitation (asthma/COPD); a fixed focal monophonic wheeze suggests localized bronchial obstruction; predominantly inspiratory noise over the neck is stridor.
examine.prerequisites: Patient able to take deep and forced breaths; quiet setting.
examine.title: Wheezing on auscultation (diffuse expiratory vs focal/monophonic)

examine.changes_what: Present: escalate now (continuous monitoring, blood gas, bronchodilator/NIV or airway plan). Absent: do not use to downgrade severity; rely on oximetry, gas and peak flow.
examine.contraindications: None; it is observation only. Do not delay oxygen, bronchodilator or airway management to complete the assessment.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use absence of the sign to withhold escalation in a drowsy, exhausted or silent-chest patient.
examine.escalation_warning: Accessory muscle use plus inability to speak, drowsiness, silent chest, bradycardia or SpO2 <90% = life-threatening exacerbation: immediate senior/ICU involvement.
examine.how: Observe from the doorway before touching the patient: sternocleidomastoid/scalene contraction on inspiration, suprasternal or intercostal retraction, tripod posture, pursed-lip exhalation, and diaphoresis. Ask an open question and note whether the patient can finish a sentence in one breath (sentences vs phrases vs single words).
examine.negative_finding: Absence of accessory muscle use does not exclude significant airflow limitation or hypercapnia; a tiring or obtunded patient may lose the sign as ventilatory failure develops.
examine.pitfalls: Loss of accessory muscle use with rising drowsiness signals fatigue, not improvement. Obesity, a thick neck and supine positioning hide sternocleidomastoid contraction.
examine.positive_finding: Visible accessory muscle use, tripoding or speech limited to words/phrases marks a severe exacerbation of airflow obstruction (asthma/COPD) or another cause of high work of breathing, and in admitted asthmatics is associated with a markedly lower %FEV1. Treat it as a severity marker, not as a discriminator between causes.
examine.prerequisites: Patient undressed enough to see the neck and chest wall; observe at rest before any intervention if safe to do so.
examine.title: Work of breathing: accessory muscle use, tripoding, pursed-lip breathing, inability to speak full sentences

examine.changes_what: Desaturation or incomplete walk: keep in hospital, escalate imaging (CTPA/HRCT/echo) and oxygen. Normal walk: supports outpatient pathway if resting evaluation is also reassuring.
examine.contraindications: Unstable angina or ACS in evolution, resting hypoxia or hypotension, suspected severe aortic stenosis with exertional syncope, untreated suspected PE with hemodynamic compromise, resting HR >120 or uncontrolled arrhythmia (contraindications adapted from ERS/ATS 6MWT standard).
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not walk a patient with resting hypoxia, hypotension, ongoing chest pain, suspected severe aortic stenosis or an untreated high-probability PE.
examine.escalation_warning: SpO2 falling below 88-90%, chest pain, presyncope or a heart-rate surge with symptoms means stop, sit the patient, give oxygen and escalate.
examine.how: Record resting SpO2, heart rate and dyspnea (Borg) with a well-fitting finger probe. Walk the patient along a flat corridor at their own pace for 1-6 minutes (or a set distance, e.g. 40 steps) with continuous oximetry; note nadir SpO2, heart-rate rise, symptom reproduction, and whether they can complete the walk. A fall in SpO2 of >=4% or to <90% is the usual desaturation criterion.
examine.negative_finding: Completing a corridor walk without desaturation or symptom reproduction lowers concern for a significant exertional gas-exchange defect but has no validated accuracy for excluding PE, ACS or aortic stenosis.
examine.pitfalls: Motion artefact, poor perfusion and nail polish produce spurious dips; a short walk may be too little stimulus and a test at the bedside is less reproducible than a standardised 6MWT (two tests recommended). Deconditioning and pain limit completion without implying cardiopulmonary disease.
examine.positive_finding: Exertional desaturation or reproduced dyspnea with a normal resting SpO2 indicates a gas-exchange or cardiopulmonary limit (ILD, pneumonia, PE, heart failure, COPD) and argues against anxiety/hyperventilation; failure to complete the walk from symptoms is a marker of severity and unsafe discharge.
examine.prerequisites: Stable resting vitals, no ongoing chest pain, ECG reviewed if chest pain or syncope is the presentation; a chair and staff available; oximeter with good waveform.
examine.title: Bedside walk / ambulatory desaturation and dyspnea reproduction test (hallway walk with pulse-ox, ability to complete)

examine.changes_what: Bilateral: pursue spirometry/COPD; unilateral with breath-sound loss: obtain CXR or POCUS for pneumothorax now; normal: no change in probability.
examine.contraindications: None; avoid delaying decompression for percussion in a hypotensive patient with suspected tension pneumothorax.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use percussion to exclude pneumothorax in trauma or after a procedure; image instead.
examine.escalation_warning: Unilateral hyperresonance with absent breath sounds, hypotension or tracheal deviation = tension pneumothorax; decompress before imaging.

evidence.citation: Oshaug K, Halvorsen PA, Melbye H. Should chest examination be reinstated in the early diagnosis of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease? Int J Chron Obstruct Pulmon Dis. 2013.
evidence.population: 375 primary-care patients aged >=40 y with a previous diagnosis of asthma or COPD (cross-sectional, Norway)

evidence.citation: Oshaug K, Halvorsen PA, Melbye H. Should chest examination be reinstated in the early diagnosis of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease? Int J Chron Obstruct Pulmon Dis. 2013.
evidence.population: Same 375 primary-care patients aged >=40 y with previous asthma/COPD diagnosis
evidence.reference_standard: Post-bronchodilator spirometry (severe COPD definition per Table 4)
evidence.target_condition: Severe COPD (post-bronchodilator spirometry threshold as defined in Table 4)

examine.how: With the patient sitting, percuss symmetric points over both lung fields anteriorly and posteriorly, comparing side to side; hyperresonance is a louder, lower-pitched, more drum-like note than normal resonance. Note whether it is bilateral (hyperinflation) or unilateral (air in the pleural space), and combine with breath-sound asymmetry.
examine.negative_finding: Normal percussion note does not exclude COPD (sensitivity about 0.2) or a small pneumothorax; the sign is a rule-in, not a rule-out, finding.
examine.pitfalls: Obesity, a thick chest wall and examiner skill blunt the sign; interobserver agreement for percussion is poor. Large bullae or a contralateral effusion can mimic unilateral hyperresonance.
examine.positive_finding: Bilateral hyperresonance in a smoker strongly raises the probability of COPD (LR+ about 9.5 in primary care); unilateral hyperresonance with reduced breath sounds points to pneumothorax on that side.
examine.prerequisites: Quiet room, chest exposed, examiner able to compare with normal resonance.
examine.title: Chest percussion hyperresonance (diffuse with barrel chest = COPD; unilateral = pneumothorax)
